# MathShikkha: A Controlled Study of Answer-Only and Chain-of-Thought Supervision for Bangla Mathematical Reasoning in Small Language Models

- **Authors**: Rahma Simin Ali, Jawad Hossain
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-09
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08503>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08503v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-evaluation, reasoning-training, test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-evaluation 0.50, reasoning-training 0.50, test-time-scaling 0.50

## In one line

Compares chain-of-thought against answer-only supervision under a protocol where the two conditions differ in nothing but the training target, and finds the rationales buy nothing in-domain for strong backbones while buying 20 to 28 points out of domain -- with a human study attributing the measurable effect to language adherence and inspectability rather than to better reasoning.

## Problem

Rationale supervision is widely believed to improve reasoning in small models, but the overwhelming majority of the evidence compares chain-of-thought-tuned models against models with no fine-tuning at all rather than against a fine-tuned control. That comparison cannot separate the value of the rationales from the value of fine-tuning on the task, and it is exactly the comparison that matters for a practitioner deciding whether to pay a large token cost at inference. The setting is Bangla mathematics, where existing small models skip steps, mix languages, misread word-problem semantics or produce fluent but invalid reasoning, and where relying on a proprietary teacher at inference time is impractical.

## Contributions

- A matched comparison that isolates supervision type by holding the split, loss masking, decoding and scoring pipeline identical across conditions, together with an explicit statement of which common uncontrolled variants can reverse the sign of the measured effect.
- The in-domain finding that rationale supervision buys nothing over answer-only fine-tuning for three stronger backbones -- negative point estimates, intervals spanning zero, and a second seed in which answer-only significantly wins -- at 15 to 52 times the inference token cost.
- The out-of-domain reversal on a three-stage contamination-audited benchmark, where rationale supervision wins by 20 to 28 points for all four models and answer-only fine-tuning actively degrades three of four below their own untuned baselines.
- Evidence that the advantage scales with reasoning depth, with the answer-only condition collapsing from 56.6 to 16.7 percent across one to four reasoning steps while the rationale condition degrades gracefully.
- A human study with external adjudication and inter-annotator agreement from 0.760 to 1.000 finding no significant improvement on reasoning-content criteria, and locating the measurable effect of rationale supervision in target-language adherence and inspectability instead.
- A three-stage contamination audit including a number-and-variable-masked similarity pass that catches same-template-different-numbers leakage, reported with its one flagged case examined and dismissed by hand.

## Method

A Bangla mathematical reasoning dataset is built with teacher-generated rationales, and four 4B-to-7B students are fine-tuned under a matched protocol whose whole point is that the two conditions differ only in the assistant training target. Held constant: the train/validation split, loaded once and shared rather than regenerated per condition; response-only loss masking for both; greedy decoding for both; and a single type-safe answer-normalisation and scoring pipeline applied uniformly across every model and condition. The paper states explicitly which uncontrolled variants would confound supervision type with training and scoring differences -- full-sequence loss for one condition against response-only for the other, or stochastic decoding for one against greedy for the other -- and notes these can reverse the apparent sign of the effect. Significance uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals with 10,000 resamples applying the same resampled indices to both conditions, and exact McNemar tests on the discordant pairs of the paired test set. In-domain results are replicated under a second seed. Out-of-domain evaluation uses an external school-textbook benchmark preceded by a three-stage contamination audit against all 1,030 training problems: exact normalised-text overlap, character-level near-duplicate similarity, and similarity after masking all numbers and variables to catch same-template-different-numbers leakage. Each model's conditions are scored on the common set of items all its conditions generated. A human study then compares three conditions -- base model under rationale-style prompting, answer-only fine-tuned, and rationale fine-tuned -- across eight criteria scored by two annotators with independent external-expert adjudication.

## Results

In-domain, rationale supervision provides no significant improvement over answer-only fine-tuning for the three stronger backbones, and the point estimates are negative for all three (-2.06, -3.09, -5.15 points), with every bootstrap interval including zero and McNemar p at or above 0.17 -- despite generating 15 to 52 times more tokens (mean 382.7 against 23.2 for one model, 372.6 against 7.1 for another). The weakest 4B backbone is the exception and gains 18.56 points at p below 0.0001. The seed replication makes the null harder rather than easier to dismiss: under a second seed the same comparison gives -10.99 points at p = 0.0001, so answer-only supervision significantly wins. Out of domain the pattern inverts completely. On the contamination-audited external benchmark -- where the audit's first two stages flagged nothing, the third flagged one problem confirmed by inspection as a false positive, and maximum problem-level similarity to any training item was 0.84 with a median of 0.53 -- rationale supervision beats matched answer-only supervision for all four models by 20.14, 28.10, 27.08 and 23.61 points, all at p below 0.0001. More striking, answer-only fine-tuning drives external accuracy below the non-fine-tuned base model for three of four: 68.75 to 46.53 percent, 58.55 to 37.70, and 67.19 to 45.05, while rationale supervision preserves or improves it for all four. The advantage concentrates with reasoning depth: on one model, answer-only falls from 56.6 percent on one-step problems to 16.7 on four-step ones while rationale supervision holds 72.4 to 58.3; on another, 50.3 to 8.3 against 62.8 to 66.7. The human study is the result that constrains the interpretation. With inter-annotator agreement from 0.760 to 1.000 across eight criteria before adjudication, it finds no significant improvement of rationale supervision over the base model on the reasoning-content criteria -- arithmetic correctness, logical validity, problem grounding, answer consistency, completeness. Its measurable effects are target-language adherence and producing inspectable reasoning at all. A Bangla-specific 9B model evaluated under the identical pipeline reaches 48.80 percent with few-shot prompting, slightly above its own rationale fine-tuning at 45.36 and broadly comparable to the best of the distilled 4B-7B models at 48.11 -- so a model already instruction-tuned for the language gains least from further rationale distillation, mirroring the finding that the weakest general backbone gains most.

## Limitations

Stated or directly visible. The in-domain null is on one 291-item test set and its sign varies by seed, which the authors report rather than selecting the favourable run. Fine-tuning shows mild overfitting -- validation loss rises while training loss falls after an intermediate stage -- and the evaluated checkpoint is selected by lowest validation loss, which is a defensible choice made on the same validation split both conditions share. Some models fall slightly below the full external item count due to non-generating items, and the authors score each model on the common set its conditions all produced rather than imputing. A small fraction of one model's outputs were degenerate or truncated at the generation ceiling and are scored incorrect. Not stated but worth noticing: the two primary human annotators are co-authors, with an external expert used for adjudication rather than for independent scoring, so the reasoning-quality result rests on annotators who knew the study's structure even if not the condition labels. The rationales come from a single proprietary teacher, so 'what rationale supervision buys' here is what that teacher's Bangla rationales buy. Four backbones and 1,030 training problems in one language and one subject support the whole conclusion, and the capability-dependence thesis -- weakest backbone gains most in-domain, most language-adapted model gains least -- is an interpretation of four points.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-evaluation**: The single most useful thing here is the demonstration that in-domain accuracy cannot detect what rationale supervision buys, and that the sign of the in-domain comparison is not even stable. Three stronger backbones show negative point estimates in-domain with intervals spanning zero, and under a second seed the answer-only condition significantly wins by 10.99 points -- while the same models gain 20 to 28 points out of domain. A study reporting only in-domain results, or only one seed, could have concluded either that rationales are useless or that they are harmful, and both would have been wrong about the thing practitioners care about. The out-of-domain half also produces the archive's clearest case of a fine-tuning procedure that improves the reported metric while damaging the model: answer-only supervision drives external accuracy below the untuned base for three of four models, one falling from 68.75 to 46.53 percent. In-domain evaluation of a fine-tuned model measures fit to the training distribution and can move in the opposite direction to capability. The human study is what makes the paper more than a benchmark result. With agreement from 0.760 to 1.000 across eight criteria and external adjudication, it finds no significant improvement on any reasoning-content criterion -- arithmetic correctness, logical validity, problem grounding, completeness -- and attributes the measurable effect to target-language adherence and to producing inspectable reasoning at all. So a 20-point accuracy gain coexists with no detectable improvement in the quality of the reasoning that produced it, which sharpens the archive's standing position that final-answer accuracy is an asymmetric diagnostic. The contamination audit is worth copying: three stages, the third masking all numbers and variables to catch same-template-different-numbers leakage, with the single flagged case inspected by hand and reported as a false positive, and the maximum and median similarities given rather than only a pass/fail.
- **reasoning-training**: This is the controlled version of a comparison the literature has been making uncontrolled, and the protocol section is the contribution. The authors hold the split, the loss masking, the decoding strategy and the scoring pipeline identical across conditions, and then state plainly which common variants would confound the result -- full-sequence loss for one condition against response-only for the other, stochastic decoding for one against greedy for the other -- noting these can reverse the apparent sign. Any archived claim that rationale supervision helps should be checked against that list first. The substantive finding for training decisions is that the benefit is entirely about generalisation and is capability-dependent in a specific direction: the weakest general-purpose backbone gains 18.56 points in-domain where the three stronger ones gain nothing, and a model already instruction-tuned for the target language gains least of all, with its few-shot prompting slightly beating its own rationale fine-tuning. So rationale distillation substitutes for capability the student lacks rather than adding capability the student has -- which is the same shape as the archive's finding that RLVR sharpens toward paths the base model already had. The depth analysis is the mechanism: answer-only supervision collapses from 56.6 to 16.7 percent across one to four reasoning steps while rationale supervision degrades gracefully, so what the rationales protect is composition over several steps rather than accuracy in general. And the degradation result is a genuine warning: fine-tuning on answers alone made three of four models worse than not fine-tuning them at all, on a held-out benchmark, which is a cost that never appears in an in-domain table.
- **test-time-scaling**: A clean measurement of what rationale-shaped inference costs and when it is worth paying. Under the matched in-domain protocol, the rationale condition generates 15 to 52 times more tokens -- 382.7 against 23.2 on one model, 372.6 against 7.1 on another -- for a point estimate that is negative on three of four backbones. That is the archive's starkest example of inference-time verbosity bought and not repaid, and it is measured rather than inferred because the two conditions are otherwise identical. The condition under which the same spend becomes worthwhile is equally specific and is the useful half: out of distribution, and increasingly so with the number of reasoning steps a problem requires, where the answer-only condition falls to 16.7 and 8.3 percent on four-step problems while the rationale condition holds near 60. So the token overhead should be read as insurance against composition depth and distribution shift, not as a general accuracy purchase -- and a practitioner evaluating in-domain on shallow problems will price it wrongly in both directions. One further observation the paper makes in passing is worth keeping: fine-tuned models produce more concise rationales (roughly 370-390 tokens) than base models attempting rationale-style generation unprompted by examples, which sprawl and repeat. Length under rationale prompting is not a property of rationale generation but of whether the model has seen well-formed ones.

## Abstract

Mathematical reasoning remains challenging in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We study whether teacher-generated Bangla Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision provides benefits beyond ordinary supervised fine-tuning. We construct \textsc{MathShikkha}, a Bangla mathematical reasoning dataset with GPT-5.4-generated rationales, and fine-tune four 4B--7B student models under a matched protocol in which answer-only and CoT conditions share data splits, response-only loss masking, decoding, and scoring, differing only in the training target. In-domain, CoT provides no significant improvement over answer-only fine-tuning for three stronger backbones (paired bootstrap 95\% CIs include zero; exact McNemar $p \geq 0.17$), despite generating 15--52$\times$ more tokens, but significantly improves the weaker 4B model by 18.56 points ($p < 0.0001$). On the larger, contamination-audited BanglaMATH benchmark, this pattern reverses: CoT significantly outperforms answer-only supervision for all four models by 20.1--28.1 points (all $p < 0.0001$). Answer-only fine-tuning also reduces out-of-domain accuracy below the base model for three models, whereas CoT preserves or improves it for all four. A human study with two co-author annotators, external-expert adjudication, and Cohen's $κ= 0.76$--$1.00$ finds no significant CoT improvement over the base model on reasoning-content criteria; instead, its measurable effect is target-language adherence and producing inspectable reasoning. Overall, rationale supervision's value depends on backbone capability and distribution shift: in this setting, its main benefits are Bangla adherence, auditable reasoning, and out-of-domain robustness rather than improved in-domain reasoning validity.
